candidateRows: Worldviews should be compared only after their contents and attractions are understood, using simplicity, explanatory reach, and predictive success where applicable.
This establishes the evaluative method governing the later comparison between naturalistic and theistic accounts of ultimate reality.
After Rasmussen identifies shared inquiry tools, Oppy develops a general methodology for understanding and comparing complete worldviews before attempting advocacy.
The important worldview differences may lie at reality's causal or logical roots, where progress can come from reducing primitive terms in the fundamental account.
It redirects the comparison toward the foundational ontology and identifies primitive reduction as a principal simplicity consideration.
Oppy's claim that most ordinary and scientific commitments will be shared across the competing worldviews.
Following discussion of shared commitments about cats, particles, and history, Rasmussen isolates the fundamental level as the likely locus of disagreement.
Naturalness may be a universally instantiated category, and positing a separate natural type requires justification under a preference for ontological simplicity.
The move directly challenges whether the natural category marks a substantive ontological divide relevant to comparing the two worldviews.
At the transition to defining naturalism, Rasmussen asks whether everything might instantiate naturalness and connects that possibility to simplicity.
The natural category historically designated a restricted created realm, and later naturalists retained it while denying the additional entities posited by Christian theory.
It supplies Oppy's substantive basis for treating natural reality as a restricted category rather than a universal property of everything.
Rasmussen's suggestion that naturalness could be a universal type whose separate inclusion creates unnecessary complexity.
Oppy traces the natural and non-natural distinction through Christian theology, Aristotle-influenced cosmology, and its later adoption by naturalists.
A necessary foundational reality can remain categorically continuous with created concrete things, making the supernatural label dispensable even if the foundation is uncreated.
It argues that the proposed theistic foundation may preserve the categorical uniformity usually associated with naturalism, narrowing the worldview contrast.
Oppy's historically grounded distinction between the natural created realm and additional non-natural reality.
Rasmussen develops a single-category model in which an intelligible necessary foundation and what it produces share a concrete ontological character.
A naturalistic initial reality is necessary yet broadly continuous with the later temporal manifold, whereas some theologies introduce radical discontinuity between God and creation.
It identifies continuity and reduced ontological discontinuity as comparative advantages of Oppy's naturalistic account of ultimate reality.
Rasmussen's proposal that his necessary foundation shares one basic concrete category with created reality.
Oppy grants that both views may exhibit some uniformity but argues that his necessary initial state remains causally continuous with subsequent reality.
Among accounts of an initial necessary reality, leaving its limits open is initially simpler than positing unexplained arbitrary limits, which add theoretical complexity.
It formulates the arbitrary-limits simplicity argument that underpins Rasmussen's subsequent case for an unlimited supreme foundation.
Oppy's presentation of a necessary natural initial state that differs minimally from later physical reality.
Rasmussen compares limited, unlimited, and noncommittal accounts of the initial item and argues that specifying brute limits incurs an extra cost.
Treating the initial reality as conscious or minded is not merely removing arbitrary limitations but adding substantial structure absent from the naturalistic account.
It presents the core naturalistic complexity objection to deriving a minded theistic foundation from an allegedly simpler absence of limits.
Rasmussen's suggestion that shaving arbitrary limits from the initial item may preserve or improve theoretical simplicity.
Oppy asks which properties the foundational item receives and argues that mentality represents positive additional content rather than mere limit removal.

Removing limits on the necessary foundation's value yields supreme value and its consequent attributes without multiplying fundamental commitments, potentially making supremacy simpler than arbitrary limitation.
This is Rasmussen's principal positive argument that a supreme theistic foundation can rival or exceed naturalism in fundamental simplicity.
Oppy's objection that mentality and other divine characteristics add structure rather than merely removing arbitrary limits.
Rasmussen treats necessary existence as value-making, derives supreme value by removing limits, and argues that consequences do not themselves increase fundamental complexity.
A simple characterization such as supremacy or perfection does not automatically entail the rich classical divine attributes, so the claimed deductions require substantial additional work.
It attacks the inferential bridge needed for Rasmussen's simple supreme foundation to generate a recognizably theistic account of ultimate reality.
Rasmussen's claim that supreme value simply characterizes the foundation and entails further supreme-making attributes.
Oppy cites skepticism about deriving determinate attributes from perfection or maximal greatness and maintains that the sparse description lacks the required consequences.
A bare characterization of perfection or supremacy does not yet establish the substantive divine attributes and consequences the theistic account requires.
This challenges the inferential bridge from a simple supreme foundation to the attributes that give the theistic worldview its explanatory and predictive content.
Rasmussen's claim that a basic notion of perfection can yield substantive divine attributes and predictions.
After Rasmussen appeals to a nonmodal idealization of value, Oppy argues that substantial additional work is needed before classical attributes can be derived from such a sparse foundation.
Supreme value plausibly entails necessary existence, logical and moral structure, resources for conscious moral beings, and the absence of unjustified evil.
The move states the principal predictive content by which the proposed theistic foundation is meant to explain logic, morality, mind, and evil while accepting evidential risk.
Oppy's objection that supremacy alone may not yield the classical attributes or needed explanatory consequences.
Rasmussen answers the demand for further derivation by listing proposed consequences of supreme value and stressing that the evil prediction exposes the theory to possible disconfirmation.
The properties and possible limits of the necessary initial reality should be left open pending science, and necessity itself terminates the demand for further explanation.
This supplies the naturalistic alternative's epistemic posture and rejects the claim that an initial necessary reality must already receive a rich positive characterization.
The preceding request for Oppy's position on whether the initial reality has fundamental or arbitrary limits.
Oppy declines to specify the initial reality beyond what inquiry can support, questions whether necessity and arbitrariness fit together, and treats necessity as an explanatory stopping point.
Necessary existence need not end explanation because a necessary entity's particular features may still call for deeper unification, and unexplained necessities add theoretical complexity.
This defends continued explanation beyond bare necessity and grounds the pro side's preference for a simpler, more unified ultimate foundation rather than brute necessary features.
Oppy's claim that necessity is where explanation ends and that no further answer to why it is necessary is available.
Rasmussen uses mathematical and concrete analogies to argue that necessary but limited features can remain explanatorily primitive, making a theory worse than one that unifies those features.
If both worldviews posit a necessary origin, they incur the same basic explanatory commitment, absent a reason to prefer brute necessity over brute contingency or vice versa.
This neutralizes an alleged comparative cost by arguing that necessary origination is common ground and therefore cannot by itself favor the theistic foundation.
Rasmussen's argument that each unexplained necessity is an added primitive that increases a worldview's complexity.
Oppy distinguishes debates over brute contingency from the shared assumption of a necessary origin and argues that, given the latter assumption, the rival views break even.
Final physics may eliminate arbitrary constants, but present ignorance about the initial state prevents judging whether its properties contain arbitrary limits or imply supremacy.
This connects the naturalistic position to theory development in physics while withholding the inference from absence of arbitrary constants to a supreme personal foundation.
Rasmussen's request to determine whether the initial reality has basic limits, lacks them, or possesses a supreme nature.
Oppy compares alleged arbitrary limits with constants inserted by hand in incomplete physical theories, while maintaining that current evidence does not decide how a final theory will look.
The causally initial physical reality need not be the sole foundation of logic, value, consciousness, or evil, since necessary domains may have independent foundations.
This directly contests the theistic unification strategy by denying that the physical beginning must also ground every logical, moral, mental, and axiological fact.
After agreement about shared logical and probabilistic resources, Oppy separates causal initiality from total fundamentality and suggests that necessary domains may not need one common ground.
Even necessary truths gain explanatory value from derivation through a smaller and more unified basis, so ultimate explanation should likewise favor foundational unification.
This provides the core comparative rationale for preferring one supreme foundation over several independent necessary domains: greater explanatory unity with fewer primitives.
Oppy's proposal that logic, morality, consciousness, and the causal initial state may rest on independent foundations.
Rasmussen argues that mathematical practice seeks basic axioms even for necessary truths and extends that preference for unified derivation to a theory of ultimate reality.
A supreme mental foundation would fall outside Oppy's naturalism without adding a simplicity cost, because specifying arbitrary limits carries at least as much information as removing them.
The move links the arbitrary-limits principle to supreme mind, explains why that result conflicts with the relevant naturalism, and answers a central simplicity objection.
The earlier concern that excluding naturalism through a supreme personal foundation may impose extra ontological or theoretical complexity.
Rasmussen distinguishes asserting limits, denying limits, and remaining noncommittal, arguing that a limitless supreme mind is not informationally costlier than a specifically limited foundation.
Worldview simplicity must be assessed across all downstream commitments and consequences, not merely by comparing how simply each view characterizes its initial reality.
This reframes the central comparison at the whole-worldview level and blocks a victory based solely on the apparent simplicity of one foundational entity's description.
Rasmussen's claim that removing arbitrary limits yields a supreme mind without increasing the informational complexity of the foundation.
Oppy argues that differences in an initial entity matter only through their broader commitments, while uncertainty about that entity makes the overall simplicity comparison difficult to complete.
Removing arbitrary limits supports a supreme nature and ultimately personhood, which naturalism would preclude.
The inference connects the arbitrary-limits principle directly to a personal supreme foundation and distinguishes that conclusion from naturalism.
The preceding question asks whether naturalism imposes an arbitrary nonmental limit on the foundation.
After discussion of how naturalism defines the foundation, Josh affirms that eliminating arbitrary limits leads toward supremacy and personhood.
Assigning consciousness a value of zero is not arbitrary, so eliminating arbitrary limits does not yield a conscious foundation.
This supplies the principal naturalistic answer to the claim that a nonmental foundation represents an objectionably arbitrary limitation.
Josh's preceding inference treats removal of arbitrary limits as supporting a supreme personal foundation.
Graham distinguishes zero and infinity from intermediate values and argues that zero consciousness can be principled rather than arbitrary.
Direct introspection and awareness of distinctions show that consciousness cannot be reduced to patterns of physical particles.
The argument links the irreducibility of conscious experience to the predictive resources of a mental supreme foundation rather than a nonmental source.
Josh develops introspection and direct discrimination as epistemic powers, applies them to conscious qualities, and connects irreducible mind to foundational theism.
Consciousness is identical with appropriately situated neural processing, and introspection does not count against that identity theory.
This is the naturalistic account of consciousness offered against the proposed irreducibility of mind and its alleged support for a mental foundation.
Josh argues from introspective access and perceived distinctions to the irreducibility of consciousness to physical patterns.
Graham maintains that mental activity just is neural functioning with appropriate environmental and evolutionary relations, while rejecting reduction and elimination labels.
Certainty about one's thoughts differs from probabilistic belief in neural structures, undermining the claim that mental and neural attributes are identical.
The move presses the epistemic and qualitative distinction at the heart of Josh's resistance to identifying conscious attributes with physical attributes.
Graham claims that introspective considerations do not bear against a neural identity theory of consciousness.
Josh contrasts immediate certainty about an occurrent thought with inferential belief about a brain and proposes one substance bearing distinct mental and physical attributes.
Distinguishing experiential content from the processing itself preserves neural identity, which is supported by broader behavioral and neurological evidence.
It answers the immediate-access objection while supplying independent empirical grounds for treating consciousness as neural processing.
Josh argues that direct awareness of thoughts and only inferential access to brains makes mental-neural identity implausible.
Graham separates what an experience represents from what the experience is, then appeals to behavior, animal evidence, neural injury, and explanatory economy.
Token identity can allow one process to instantiate both neural and conscious properties without reducing conscious qualities to physical types.
The distinction refines the disagreement by allowing physical realization while preserving the nonidentity of phenomenal and physical property types.
Graham presents consciousness as wholly identical with neural processing and denies that Josh's distinctions challenge that view.
Josh suggests partial agreement through token identity while maintaining that first-person phenomenal aspects are not simply shapes, functions, or physical matter.
Phenomenal knowledge requires undergoing the relevant neural state because the conscious experience simply is that processing, not something constituted by it.
The response clarifies that Graham's position asserts strict identity and uses experiential knowledge cases to explain why occupying the neural state matters.
Josh proposes token identity with distinct phenomenal and physical property types as a possible point of agreement.
Graham resists translating his view into Josh's type-token formulation and explains phenomenal acquaintance as being in the relevant neural-processing state.
Identifying feelings, thoughts, and logical relations with physical patterns appears as contradictory as identifying opposed qualities.
This crystallizes the pro side's basic conceivability and introspective resistance to strict type identity between conscious qualities and physical patterns.
Graham insists that conscious experience is strictly identical with neural processing rather than constituted or produced by it.
Josh tests strict identity against examples of emotions, curiosity, entailment, and thoughts, reporting that the proposed identities appear fundamentally mismatched.
Local advantages between worldviews are unimportant unless they survive comparison of the complete worldviews and all relevant data.
The move states the governing comparative methodology for deciding whether naturalism or theism provides the better overall account of reality.
Graham argues that carefully selected evidence can favor either worldview in one respect, so isolated advantages should not decide the overall comparison.
Examining one property at a time remains valuable for achieving clarity, provided it is not treated as sufficient to win a contest between whole worldviews.
The move directly qualifies the whole-worldview methodology at issue by defending focused comparisons as necessary intermediate inquiries into simplicity and predictive success.
Oppy's position that isolated advantages are uninteresting or misleading unless competing worldviews are assessed in their entirety.

After Oppy criticizes arguments based on isolated advantages and unsupported all-else-equal assumptions, Rasmussen agrees about contest-oriented inference but defends property-by-property inquiry as a tool for clarity.
Shared commitments allow some narrowing of worldview comparison, but they still leave an enormous body of relevant disagreement that focused examples do not capture.
This qualification preserves Oppy's central methodological objection while conceding that common sense, science, and other shared commitments can be removed from the comparison.
Rasmussen's defense of isolating one property at a time to clarify simplicity, predictive success, and other comparative considerations.

Rasmussen argues that presenting every feature of a worldview would distract from focused inquiry. Oppy replies that agreed material can be set aside, yet substantial worldview-level differences remain.
The simplicity question becomes harder under sustained examination, and the no-arbitrary-limits proposal remains subject to unresolved surrounding considerations.
The closing reflection bears on two major disputed tools in the debate—simplicity and arbitrary limits—by withholding resolution and identifying the need for further analysis.
Rasmussen's use of simplicity and the no-arbitrary-limits principle to support a supreme foundational reality over restricted alternatives.

During closing reflections, Rasmussen lists clarification about naturalness, arbitrary limits, and identity. Oppy then reports that simplicity looks increasingly difficult and that the arbitrary-limits argument remains unsettled.
